about: The scripted AI lesson for p4-nuclear-model (2026-11-27, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p2-static and p3-density.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about what is inside an atom, and how scientists found out without ever seeing one.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Two objects both have a positive charge. What do they do to each other?
steps.right: Yes: like charges repel, so two positive charges push each other away.

wrong.other: Not quite: they repel. Like charges push each other away.
wrong.attract: Not quite: opposite charges attract. Two positive charges are alike, so they repel: they push each other away.
wrong.nothing: Not quite: charges always push or pull on each other. Two positive charges are alike, so they repel.

idk.hint: Opposite charges pull together. Two positive charges are not opposite: they are the same kind.

steps.answerWhy: Like charges repel, so two positive charges push each other away.

steps.question: Second: a small lead weight and a big cork have the same mass. Which is denser?
steps.right: Yes: the lead packs the same mass into a much smaller space.

wrong.other: Not quite: the lead weight. Same mass in less space means denser.
wrong.cork: Not quite: the cork spreads its mass through more space. The lead packs the same mass into a small space, so it is denser.
wrong.same: Not quite: density is mass in each cm³, not mass alone. The lead fits the same mass into less space, so it is denser.

idk.hint: Dense means a lot of mass in a small space. The lead weight is the smaller of the two.

steps.answerWhy: The lead weight has the same mass in a smaller space, so it is denser.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Everything is made of atoms. An atom is far too small to see, even with a microscope.
Scientists cannot look inside an atom, so they use a model: a picture or idea that explains what they cannot see. When new evidence does not fit a model, the model is changed.
About 200 years ago, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided into anything smaller.
Then, in 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron: a tiny particle with a negative charge. It came from inside atoms, so atoms could be divided after all.

steps.question: An atom has no overall charge, yet it contains negative electrons. What else must an atom contain?
steps.right: Yes: positive charge must balance the negative electrons, so the atom has no overall charge.

wrong.other: Not quite: some positive charge, to balance the electrons.
wrong.more: Not quite: more electrons would make it more negative. To cancel the negative charge, the atom must also hold positive charge.
wrong.nothing: Not quite: electrons alone would give the atom a negative charge. Something positive must cancel it out.

idk.hint: The electrons are negative, but the atom is not. A negative charge is cancelled by the opposite kind.

steps.answerWhy: The negative electrons must be balanced by positive charge, so the atom has no overall charge.

steps.text: Thomson's answer, in 1904: the atom is a ball of positive charge, spread out evenly. The electrons are dotted through it, like plums in a pudding. This is called the plum pudding model.

steps.question: A pupil draws the plum pudding model with all the positive charge in one small dot in the middle. What is wrong with the drawing?

options.text: The electrons should be in the dot too
Nothing: that is the plum pudding model
The positive charge should fill the whole atom

steps.right: Yes: the positive charge is the pudding, spread through the whole atom, with no central dot.

wrong.other: Not quite: the positive charge should fill the whole atom.
wrong.electrons: Not quite: in the plum pudding model there is no central dot at all. The positive charge is spread through the whole atom, like the pudding.
wrong.nothing: Not quite: a small central dot of charge is a later idea. In the plum pudding model the positive charge fills the whole atom, like the pudding.

idk.hint: In the model, the positive charge is the pudding. A pudding is not a small dot: it fills the bowl.

steps.answerWhy: In the plum pudding model, the positive charge is spread through the whole atom, with no central dot.

steps.prompt: In one line: what did the plum pudding model say an atom is like?
points: the atom is a ball of positive charge, spread out evenly
negative electrons are dotted through it
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the plum pudding model said an atom is a ball of spread-out positive charge, with negative electrons dotted through it.

steps.text: A good model predicts what an experiment will show. In 1909, Geiger and Marsden, working with Ernest Rutherford, tested the plum pudding model.
The test used alpha particles: tiny, fast particles with a positive charge. They come from a radioactive source, a material whose atoms give them out on their own. The next lesson is about these.

Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil. A screen flashed where each one landed. Particles sent off in different directions are scattered, so this is the alpha particle scattering experiment.
In the plum pudding model, the positive charge is spread thinly through the whole atom. So it could only give a fast alpha particle a weak push.

steps.question: If the plum pudding model were right, what would the alpha particles do?

options.text: All get stuck in the foil
Nearly all go straight through, barely turned

steps.right: Yes: a weak push hardly turns a fast particle, so nearly all would go straight through.

wrong.other: Not quite: nearly all would go straight through, barely turned.
wrong.back: Not quite: a weak push cannot turn a fast particle right round. Nearly all would go straight through, barely turned.
wrong.stuck: Not quite: the foil is very thin and the push is weak. So nearly all would go straight through, barely turned.

idk.hint: A weak push cannot turn a fast particle round. One option has the particles hardly turned at all.

steps.answerWhy: The spread-out positive charge could only push weakly, so nearly all alpha particles would go straight through.

steps.text: What really happened? Most alpha particles did go straight through the foil.

steps.question: What does that first result tell you about an atom?

options.text: Most of it is empty space
The foil had holes in it

steps.right: Yes: most of an atom is empty space.

wrong.other: Not quite: most of an atom is empty space.
wrong.nocharge: Not quite: it does have charge, as the next results show. Most particles went straight through because most of the atom is empty space.
wrong.holes: Not quite: the foil was a solid sheet of gold atoms. The particles passed through the atoms themselves, so most of an atom is empty space.

idk.hint: A particle that meets nothing goes straight on. Think about what most of the atom must be.

steps.answerWhy: Most alpha particles went straight through, so most of an atom is empty space.

steps.text: Deflected means pushed off a straight path.

But a few alpha particles were deflected through large angles. So the positive charge is not spread out: it is packed into a small region at the centre, which repels the positive alpha particles strongly.
And a very small number bounced almost straight back. Only something tiny and very dense could do that. Rutherford called this tiny, dense, positive centre the nucleus.
The picture shows these results around one nucleus. It is not to scale: a real nucleus is far smaller than this.

steps.question: Why did only a very few alpha particles bounce back?

options.text: Only those that hit an electron
Only those heading almost straight at the nucleus

steps.right: Yes: the nucleus is tiny, so very few alpha particles head straight at it. Those are repelled back before they reach it.

wrong.other: Not quite: only those heading almost straight at the tiny nucleus.
wrong.electron: Not quite: electrons are far too light to turn an alpha particle back. Only the few heading almost straight at the tiny, positive nucleus were pushed back.
wrong.slow: Not quite: it was about aim, not speed. The nucleus is tiny, so only the few heading almost straight at it were pushed back.

idk.hint: The nucleus is tiny, so most alpha particles miss it by a long way. One option is about aiming at it.

steps.answerWhy: The nucleus is so tiny that only a very few alpha particles head almost straight at it, and those are repelled back.

steps.text: The plum pudding model could not explain this evidence, so scientists replaced it. The new model has a tiny, positive nucleus at the centre, with the electrons around it. It is called the nuclear model.

steps.prompt: In one line: what did the alpha particles that bounced back show?
points: there is a tiny nucleus at the centre of the atom
the nucleus holds the positive charge
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the alpha particles that bounced back showed there is a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre of the atom, holding its positive charge.

keyPoints.heading: Structure of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons

steps.text: Now the nuclear model in numbers. An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. That is standard form: it means 0.0000000001 m.
The radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom.

steps.question: The nucleus is tiny, but it sent alpha particles back. Where is most of the mass of an atom?
steps.right: Yes: most of the mass of an atom is in its tiny, dense nucleus.

wrong.other: Not quite: in the nucleus.
wrong.electrons: Not quite: electrons have very little mass. Only something dense could send alpha particles back: most of the mass is packed into the tiny nucleus.
wrong.spread: Not quite: that was the plum pudding idea. In the nuclear model, most of the mass is packed into the tiny nucleus.

idk.hint: The particles that came back were pushed by something dense, packed into a tiny space.

steps.answerWhy: Most of the mass of an atom is in its tiny, dense nucleus.

steps.text: The nucleus is made of two kinds of particle. A proton is a particle with a positive charge.
A neutron is a particle with no charge. Protons and neutrons are both in the nucleus; the electrons are outside it.

Relative mass compares each particle's mass with a proton's, which counts as 1. A neutron has the same mass as a proton, so its relative mass is 1 too. An electron is far lighter: its relative mass is very small, almost 0.
Relative charge compares charges in the same way. A proton has relative charge +1, a neutron 0 and an electron −1.

steps.question: A particle has relative mass 1 and relative charge +1. Which particle is it?
steps.right: Yes: a proton has relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.

wrong.other: Not quite: a proton.
wrong.neutron: Not quite: a neutron has relative mass 1 but no charge. With charge +1, it is a proton.
wrong.electron: Not quite: an electron has charge −1 and almost no mass. Mass 1 and charge +1 is a proton.

idk.hint: Two particles have relative mass 1. Only one of those has a charge.

steps.answerWhy: A proton has relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.

steps.text: The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number. It decides which element the atom is, such as carbon or gold: every carbon atom has 6 protons.
The number of protons plus neutrons is the mass number. So the number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: Carbon-12 has atomic number 6 and mass number 12. How many neutrons does it have?
steps: Write the rule: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

steps.question: Your turn. An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
steps.right: Yes: 12. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

wrong.other: Not quite: 12. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
wrong.add: Not quite: 12. Subtract, do not add: neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
wrong.mass: Not quite: 12. The mass number counts protons and neutrons together. Take away the 11 protons: 23 − 11 = 12.
wrong.protons: Not quite: 12. 11 is the number of protons. Neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12.

idk.hint: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Work out 23 − 11.

steps.answerWhy: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

steps.text: The picture shows a lithium atom, not to scale: 3 protons and 4 neutrons in the middle, 3 electrons around. Its atomic number is 3 and its mass number is 7.
An atom has as many electrons as protons. The +1s and −1s cancel, so an atom has no overall charge.

If an atom loses an electron, it has one more proton than electrons, so it has an overall positive charge. A particle with an overall charge is called an ion. A lithium atom that loses one electron is written Li⁺.

steps.question: A sodium atom gains one electron. What overall charge does it now have?
steps.right: Yes: one extra electron makes it a negative ion.

wrong.other: Not quite: negative.
wrong.positive: Not quite: it now has one more electron than protons, and electrons are negative. So its overall charge is negative.
wrong.none: Not quite: it now has one more electron than protons, so the charges no longer cancel. Its overall charge is negative.

idk.hint: Electrons are negative. After gaining one, it has more electrons than protons.

steps.answerWhy: Gaining an electron gives the atom more electrons than protons, so it becomes a negative ion.

steps.text: The symbol for an atom shows both numbers. For carbon-12 it is ¹²₆C. The mass number, 12, is at the top. The atomic number, 6, is at the bottom.

steps.question: U is the symbol for uranium. How many protons does a uranium atom ²³⁸₉₂U have?
steps.right: Yes: 92, the bottom number, the atomic number.

wrong.other: Not quite: 92, the bottom number.
wrong.mass: Not quite: 238 is the mass number, at the top: protons plus neutrons. The protons are the bottom number, 92.
wrong.neutrons: Not quite: 146 is the number of neutrons, 238 − 92. The protons are the bottom number, 92.

idk.hint: The atomic number counts the protons, and it is the bottom number.

steps.answerWhy: The bottom number is the atomic number, which counts the protons: 92.

steps.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8.

steps.question: O is oxygen, N is nitrogen, C is carbon and S is sulfur. Which pair are isotopes of the same element?
steps.right: Yes: both have 8 protons, so both are oxygen, but they have 8 and 10 neutrons.

wrong.other: Not quite: ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O.
wrong.samemass: Not quite: these share a mass number, but their atomic numbers differ, so they are different elements. ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O both have 8 protons.
wrong.double: Not quite: 16 protons is a different element from 8 protons. ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O both have 8 protons.

idk.hint: Isotopes have the same number of protons, so look for the same bottom number.

steps.answerWhy: Isotopes have the same atomic number (bottom number) but different mass numbers: ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O.

steps.prompt: In one line: what are isotopes?
points: atoms with the same number of protons
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: isotopes are atoms of the same element, with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

keyPoints.heading: Energy levels and later changes to the model

steps.text: Niels Bohr improved the nuclear model. He said the electrons orbit the nucleus only at certain fixed distances. His calculations agreed with the results of experiments.
Each fixed distance is an energy level. The further a level is from the nucleus, the higher its energy.
Electromagnetic radiation is energy that travels as waves, like light. Radio waves and X-rays are other kinds.
When an electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation, it takes in energy and moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.

steps.question: To move the other way, down to a lower energy level, what must an electron do?
steps.right: Yes: moving down a level, the electron gives out energy as electromagnetic radiation.

wrong.other: Not quite: emit electromagnetic radiation.
wrong.absorb: Not quite: absorbing gives an electron energy and moves it up. To move down it must give energy out: it emits radiation.
wrong.nucleus: Not quite: it stays outside the nucleus, on a lower level. To move down it gives energy out: it emits radiation.

idk.hint: Moving up takes energy in. Moving down is the opposite, so energy goes out.

steps.answerWhy: To move to a lower energy level, an electron gives out energy: it emits electromagnetic radiation.

steps.text: The picture shows both moves: absorbing takes the electron up a level, and emitting brings it down.

The protons and neutrons you met earlier were found after Rutherford's nucleus. Experiments showed that the positive charge of a nucleus is made of a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same charge: the protons.
About 20 years after the nucleus was accepted, James Chadwick's experiments showed that the nucleus also holds neutrons.

steps.question: Which model came straight after the plum pudding model?

options.text: The nuclear model, with a tiny nucleus
Tiny spheres that cannot be divided

steps.right: Yes: the scattering results led scientists to replace the plum pudding model with the nuclear model.

wrong.other: Not quite: the nuclear model.
wrong.bohr: Not quite: Bohr improved the nuclear model, so his came later. Straight after the plum pudding came Rutherford's nuclear model.
wrong.spheres: Not quite: that idea came before the electron was found. Straight after the plum pudding came the nuclear model.

idk.hint: The scattering experiment found the nucleus. One option has a nucleus but no energy levels yet.

steps.answerWhy: The scattering results led scientists to replace the plum pudding model with the nuclear model; Bohr improved that later.

steps.prompt: In one line: why has the model of the atom changed over time?
points: experiments found new evidence the old model could not explain
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the model of the atom changed each time experiments found new evidence the old model could not explain.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: in the scattering experiment, what did most alpha particles do?
steps.right: Yes: most went straight through, so most of an atom is empty space.

wrong.other: Not quite: most went straight through.
wrong.w1: Not quite: only a very few bounced back. Most went straight through, because most of an atom is empty space.
wrong.w2: Not quite: most went straight through, because most of an atom is empty space.

steps.answerWhy: Most alpha particles went straight through, so most of an atom is empty space.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: ²⁷₁₃Al is an aluminium atom. How many neutrons does it have?
steps.right: Yes: 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons.

wrong.other: Not quite: 14. Neutrons = 27 − 13 = 14.

steps.answerWhy: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: what is the relative charge of a neutron?
steps.right: Yes: 0. A neutron has no charge.

wrong.other: Not quite: 0.
wrong.w1: Not quite: +1 is a proton. A neutron has no charge: 0.
wrong.w2: Not quite: −1 is an electron. A neutron has no charge: 0.

steps.answerWhy: A neutron has no charge, so its relative charge is 0.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: Cl is chlorine, Ar is argon and Ca is calcium. Which pair are isotopes of the same element?
steps.right: Yes: both have 17 protons, but 18 and 20 neutrons.

wrong.other: Not quite: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl.
wrong.w1: Not quite: different atomic numbers, 18 and 20, so different elements. ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl both have 17 protons.
wrong.w2: Not quite: different atomic numbers, 17 and 18, so different elements. ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl both have 17 protons.

steps.answerWhy: Isotopes have the same atomic number: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl both have 17 protons.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: an electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation. Where does it go?

options.text: To a lower energy level, closer in
To a higher energy level, further out

steps.right: Yes: absorbing moves it up, further from the nucleus.

wrong.other: Not quite: to a higher energy level, further out.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is what happens when it emits radiation. Absorbing moves it up, further from the nucleus.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it stays outside the nucleus. Absorbing moves it up a level, further out.

steps.answerWhy: Absorbing electromagnetic radiation moves an electron to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: what did Bohr add to the nuclear model?

options.text: Positive charge spread through the atom

steps.right: Yes: Bohr put the electrons at fixed distances, called energy levels.

wrong.other: Not quite: electrons at fixed distances.
wrong.w1: Not quite: the nucleus came from the scattering experiment. Bohr added electrons at fixed distances: energy levels.
wrong.w2: Not quite: that was the plum pudding model. Bohr added electrons at fixed distances: energy levels.

steps.answerWhy: Bohr said electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances: energy levels.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
